findings.endpoint: cognitive function scale in mild cognitive impairment
findings.population: Japanese adults aged 50-80 with mild cognitive impairment (n=30)
findings.frequency: daily (four 250 mg tablets three times a day)
findings.finding_summary: In this double-blind placebo-controlled trial, the Hericium erinaceus group showed significantly increased cognitive function scale scores versus placebo at weeks 8, 12, and 16, with laboratory tests showing no adverse effects.
findings.limitations: single trial of 30 subjects; dry-powder tablets rather than a standardized extract

findings.population: participants with Alzheimer's disease (20 RCTs, 1,823 participants)
findings.finding_summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 randomized trials (1,823 participants) reported significant improvement in cognitive function versus placebo on the Mini-Mental State Examination at 8, 12, and 16 weeks.
findings.limitations: the methodological quality of most included trials had a high risk of bias; the authors advise cautious interpretation

findings.endpoint: activities of daily living in Alzheimer's disease
findings.population: participants with Alzheimer's disease (20 RCTs, 1,823 participants)
findings.finding_summary: The same meta-analysis reported that activities of daily living favored huperzine A at 6, 12, and 16 weeks, with no severe adverse events reported in the trials.
findings.limitations: same high risk-of-bias caveat as the cognitive endpoint

findings.endpoint: cognitive decline in mild cognitive impairment and mild Alzheimer's disease
findings.population: patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild Alzheimer's disease
findings.finding_summary: This meta-analysis of double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trials concluded that acetyl-L-carnitine improves mild cognitive impairment, prevents deterioration, and is well tolerated.
findings.limitations: DARE appraisal cautioned that pooling across different measurement instruments may not be reliable and the clinical importance of the statistically significant findings was unclear

findings.finding_summary: This Cochrane review of 16 trials found evidence of benefit on clinical global impression (and MMSE at 24 weeks) but no evidence of benefit on objective assessments in any other outcome area, concluding the evidence was insufficient to recommend routine clinical use.
findings.limitations: the authors note the statistically significant global-impression result may be due to chance given the large number of comparisons

findings.endpoint: cognitive performance under acute stress or high cognitive demand
findings.population: healthy adults in short-term stressful or cognitively demanding conditions
findings.finding_summary: This review concluded that tyrosine supplementation effectively enhances cognitive performance, particularly in short-term stressful and/or cognitively demanding situations when dopamine and/or norepinephrine is temporarily depleted.
findings.limitations: narrative review; effectiveness across individual studies varies considerably

findings.finding_summary: The same review judged the potential of tyrosine supplementation to treat clinical disorders as limited, with benefits likely determined by the presence and extent of impaired neurotransmitter function and synthesis.

findings.endpoint: cognitive decline and dementia prevention in cognitively healthy older adults
findings.population: cognitively healthy adults aged 60+ (3 RCTs, 3,536 participants)
findings.finding_summary: This Cochrane review of three randomized controlled trials (3,536 people aged 60 and over without cognitive impairment at baseline) found no benefit of omega-3 supplementation over placebo on standard mental state examinations, memory, or verbal fluency.
findings.limitations: the authors note the trials cover the short term only; longer-term effects remain unknown

findings.endpoint: episodic memory in age-related cognitive decline (MIDAS trial)
findings.population: healthy older adults (mean age 70) with mild memory complaints (n=485)
findings.finding_summary: In the MIDAS randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 900 mg/day algal DHA produced significantly fewer Paired Associate Learning errors versus placebo at 24 weeks (p=.03) and improved immediate and delayed verbal recognition memory (p<.02), but not working memory or executive function.
findings.limitations: benefits limited to episodic/recognition memory domains; industry-run trial of algal DHA

findings.endpoint: cognitive and functional decline in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease
findings.finding_summary: In this multicenter randomized trial, 2 g/day algal DHA did not slow the rate of cognitive decline (ADAS-cog) or functional decline (CDR sum of boxes) versus placebo, with no effect on activities of daily living, neuropsychiatric symptoms, or brain-atrophy rate in the MRI subsample.
findings.limitations: contrast with MIDAS suggests any DHA effect may be stage-dependent — absent once Alzheimer's disease is established

findings.endpoint: clinical global impression of change in cognitive impairment
findings.population: older adults with dementia or cognitive impairment (19 double-blind placebo-controlled studies)
findings.finding_summary: This meta-analysis of 19 double-blind placebo-controlled studies reported a significant odds ratio and favorable number needed to treat for global impression of change with piracetam versus placebo in older subjects with cognitive impairment.
findings.limitations: global-impression endpoint rather than objective cognitive measures; older heterogeneous trials with industry authorship

findings.endpoint: memory enhancement in adults with memory impairment
findings.population: adults with memory impairment (18 studies, 886 patients)
findings.finding_summary: This 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 studies (886 patients) found no significant difference in memory enhancement between piracetam and control (SMD 0.75, 95% CI -0.19 to 1.69, p=0.12), concluding the impact of piracetam on memory function cannot be definitively ascertained.
findings.limitations: very high heterogeneity (I²=96%) across included studies

findings.endpoint: overall cognitive ability composite (executive function, working memory, attention, episodic memory)
findings.population: adults aged 50-70 with self-reported cognitive complaints, anxiety, and sleep disorder
findings.finding_summary: In this randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial, magnesium L-threonate (MMFS-01) significantly improved a four-domain overall cognitive ability composite versus placebo (p=0.003, Cohen's d=0.91), with improvement evident by week 6.
findings.limitations: single-site trial run by the compound's developer; the trial's 'brain age' framing is a derived metric, not a standard endpoint — independent replication needed
